sources.title: Van 't Kruijs Opening and related pages (search snippet only)

overview: 1.e3 opens lines for the f1-bishop and the queen, claims the e4 square lightly and commits to nothing else; it blocks the c1-bishop, so White plans to free that bishop early (b3, or d4 and Nd2/Bd2). It is mainly a transposition device: c4 gives English-type positions, d4 Queen's Pawn structures, b3 Larsen's Opening, and f4 Bird-type set-ups, and 1...e5 2.e4 is a reversed Open Game. Black has maximum freedom and the opening invites him to over-commit in the centre. It is considered passive but sound and gives White no particular advantage; its popularity has declined and strong players use it mainly to reach known structures.

white_ideas.idea: Use 1.e3 as a transposition tool: English (c4), Queen's Pawn (d4), Larsen (b3), Bird-like (f4), or French reversed structures
Free the queen's bishop early because e3 blocks the c1-bishop
Develop the kingside quickly (Nf3, Be2, 0-0) and challenge a Black centre that has over-committed

black_ideas.idea: Take the centre with 1...e5 or 1...d5; keep options open with 1...Nf6 (Reti transposition) or 1...c5, or fianchetto with 1...g6
1...e5 2.e4 leads to a reversed Open Game, a curiosity

typical_structures.structure: Highly transpositional: depends on Black's central choice and White's follow-up (English, Queen's Pawn, Larsen, reversed French)

character.notes: s2 describes the play as calm (sharpness about 0.94-0.97) and the opening as passive but solid. s1 calls it a 'chameleon' and says it is not aggressive compared to 1.e4. Typical play is steady, manoeuvring, without forcing sequences.

gambit.notes: No material is given. A rare delayed Keoni-Hiva gambit appears in the input (14 games) but is not a real line.

soundness.notes: Sound. s2: passive but solid, strong players equalise; playable for White if the c1-bishop finds an active diagonal. s1: the opening remains playable for Black regardless of reply, and 1.e3 gains little except as a transposition. s3 snippet: a fine opening used even by Carlsen.

structure.notes: No fixed centre: the pawn structure depends on the transposition. Most volume goes to 1...e5 and 1...d5, where White then chooses d4 or c4/e4 set-ups. In many lines the centre stays tense or closed with e3/d4 pawns (Queen's Pawn) or open with e4 (reversed Open Game).

approach.notes: A set-up that can be played against almost anything, mainly because of its transposition value: s2 says elite players use it primarily as a transposition device; s1 says it is a 'chameleon' and ranks sixth among the twenty first moves in ChessBase. Used by Nimzowitsch, Larsen, Blatny, and even Carlsen (s1, s3). Popularity is falling: s2 reports adoption peaking at 2.35% in 2013 and falling to 1.62% in 2025 (which rating band these are is not stated). Respectable but a sideline for strong players.

level.notes: Judged for White. Little to memorise because the first move commits to no line (s1: preferred by players prioritising adaptability over theoretical depth), and s2 labels difficulty beginner level. But playing it well means knowing the structures of the English, Queen's Pawn or Larsen set-ups it transposes into, and freeing the c1-bishop. The plans come from those target openings.

plan_phrases: transposition to English, Queen's Pawn or Larsen

sublines_that_differ.name: 1.e3 e5 2.e4
sublines_that_differ.how: Reversed Open Game with Black to move; mostly a curiosity (s3).

sublines_that_differ.name: 1.e3 d5
sublines_that_differ.how: White usually plays 2.d4 or 2.c4 into Queen's Pawn or English-style set-ups; the second most played branch (26.8M games).

description.claim: 1.e3 is a highly flexible and unassuming first move that opens a line for the queen and king's bishop
It avoids early confrontation and theory, often transposing into Queen's Pawn, English or reversed French setups
description.note: s1 lists English, Queen's Pawn, French, Bird and Larsen. 'Reversed French' is s1's French Defense (1.e3 d5 2.e4 transposition).

description.claim: Perfect for creative, patient players who sidestep mainstream theory and outmanoeuvre opponents in a less-defined strategic battle
description.note: s1 says it suits players prioritising adaptability over theoretical depth; 'creative' and 'outmanoeuvre' are not sourced.

common_plans.claim: White: transpose into a favourable Queen's Pawn, English or Reti setup by playing d4, c4 and Nf3 in a flexible order
common_plans.note: c4 gives the English, d4 Queen's Pawn, b3 Larsen (s2). The Reti arises via 1...Nf6 transposition (s1).

common_plans.claim: White: develop the kingside quickly (Nf3, Be2, 0-0) then challenge Black's central control
Black: seize the centre immediately with ...d5 and ...e5 to claim a space advantage
common_plans.note: s2 lists central claims with 1...e5 or 1...d5, and notes the opening invites Black to overcommit. Both pawns at once is possible but not what the sources describe.

common_plans.claim: Black: develop pieces actively to punish White's passive opening and prevent a comfortable transposition
common_plans.note: s2 calls it passive but solid, allowing strong players to equalise, so 'punish' overstates; no source describes Black punishing it.
